en: The banana plant is a giant herb, not a tree, because its trunk consists of tightly packed leaf sheaths rather than wood.
The Philippine tarsier can rotate its head 180 degrees in each direction to spot insects in the dark without moving its body.
Sweat cools your body down because the evaporation of liquid water from your skin absorbs excess heat energy into the air.
During a butterfly's pupa stage, the caterpillar's body completely digests itself into a nutrient-rich liquid before forming adult wings and antennae.
Mangrove trees grow specialized aerial roots called pneumatophores that stick up from coastal mud to absorb oxygen directly from the air.
Carabaos wallow in mud to cool down because they lack enough sweat glands to effectively regulate their body temperature in hot weather.
The makahiya plant quickly folds its leaves when touched because a sudden loss of water pressure in its cells causes them to droop.
Whale sharks feed by swimming with their massive mouths open to filter tiny plankton and small fish out of the ocean water.
Digestion begins in the mouth when salivary amylase, an enzyme in your saliva, starts breaking down complex carbohydrates into simpler sugars.
Coral polyps build massive reef structures by secreting calcium carbonate from seawater to form hard, protective external skeletons over thousands of years.
Tadpoles breathe underwater using gills, but during metamorphosis into adult frogs, they develop lungs to breathe atmospheric oxygen on land.
Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit the dengue virus when they bite humans to drink blood, which they need to develop their eggs.
